summary.text:
Gosport BC's Treasury Management Update to Policy and Organisation Board on 26 November 2025, for noting. A single 17-page document covering the 2024/25 outturn, an in-year 2025/26 position at 30 September 2025, and the 2024/25 Prudential Indicators outturn plus a light 2025/26 update. No separate figures appendix — the tables sit in the report body itself. Appendix A is Arlingclose's generic public-sector commentary and carries nothing council-specific.

Position at 31 March 2025: £59.150m of gross borrowing, of which £57.150m PWLB at 3.65% weighted (average life 21.21 years) plus £2.000m of variable-rate local-authority money at 6.00% for a two-week average life. HRA dominates the book — £51.512m of the PWLB stock is HRA (87%), and £62.247m of the £81.385m CFR is HRA (76%). Total CFR came in £0.854m under the revised estimate on capital-programme slippage. Under-borrowing £22.235m — the balance-sheet identity closes to the pound on the assumption OLTL = £0, which the paper's own 'Total Debt' £59,150k line at page 10 is consistent with.

Position at 30 September 2025: £54.950m of borrowing (down £4.2m on year-end), all PWLB, no local-authority stock, weighted rate unchanged at 3.65%. Investments £11.560m at 30 September against £6.340m at year-start — cash growing as expected borrowing is deferred. No interim CFR is printed for 30/09/2025.

The single most distinctive disclosure in the paper is the 2024/25 Maturity Structure indicator at page 6: the 10-years-and-above bucket ran at 52% against the approved 30%–50% range — indicator NOT complied. The paper's own footnote explains the arithmetic cleanly: no borrowing over 10 years was undertaken during 2024/25 and the limits had been calibrated assuming a higher year-end stock than actually materialised. The long-dated exposure in £ terms did not grow; the total book turned out smaller than the strategy assumed, so the percentage moved against the council even though the underlying position did not. A self-disclosed indicator failure with a stated technical cause — not a governance concern, but worth writing about because it sits against the HRA discount-window closing in March 2026 and the paper's own note (page 8) that £1.8m of HRA capital programme borrowing plus refinancing of ~£6.6m of maturing HRA loans is planned inside that window.

Investment income is running well ahead of plan for H1 2025/26: £257,497 received to 30 September against a full-year budget of £186,800 — half-year receipts already 137.8% of the full-year plan. Driven by MMF balances running well above year-start (£10.230m in MMFs at end Q2 vs £6.240m at 01/04/2025); rates fell over the period (MMF 4.53% → 4.06%) so the volume effect outweighed the rate effect. Interest rate exposure indicator marked complied: a 1% rise in rates would benefit the revenue budget by £84k, because variable-rate MMF cash rises with the market while the fixed-PWLB-dominant debt cost barely moves.

Loan-book reconciliation does not tie: our bc-loans file for GOSPORT BOROUGH COUNCIL holds 18 loans totalling £51.45m at 3.69% weighted, but every loan in our file has a Start date after 30 September 2025 — filtering as-at either balance date returns zero. Same failure mode as documented at Canterbury (E07000106) and Cambridge (E07000008) — Start-field drift in bc-loans. Two specific loans on the paper's HRA refinancing table (page 4) DO match our file exactly on rate and maturity: the £5m at 4.64% and £3m at 4.52%. Kept in the note as an internal cross-check; per PIPELINE guidance the loan-book claim is kept out of the email entirely.

Draft is built from the paper's own content and does not lean on our loan-file view. Three hooks: the self-disclosed maturity indicator breach and its stated cause; the HRA discount window closing in March 2026 with £1.8m plus ~£6.6m of activity planned inside it; and the H1 investment income position ahead of the full-year budget. No officer email address is published in the paper — Nicola Nestor is named as Report Author/Lead Officer on page 12 but no contact block is printed; the 'Author' line on the front cover reads 'Head of Finance' without a name. The email is drafted; the recipient address is outstanding.

officer.body:
Dear [name],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a couple of thoughts on the Treasury Management Update taken to Policy and Organisation Board on 26 November 2025. It's a while behind us now, and this is written well ahead of the next annual cycle rather than around any live meeting. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The report is clearly written and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The piece that stood out first is the maturity indicator at page 6: the 10-years-and-above bucket ran at 52% against your 30%-50% approved range, marked not complied. The footnote explains the arithmetic cleanly — no long-dated borrowing was taken during 2024/25 and the limits had been set assuming a higher year-end stock than actually materialised — so the long-dated position in pounds didn't grow, but the denominator shrank around it and the percentage moved against you. Not a governance concern on the face of it, but a nice worked example of why percentage-of-book limits are sensitive to the size assumption behind them. On any HRA drawdowns since the report — the page-8 note flagged £1.8m of HRA capital-programme borrowing plus refinancing of ~£6.6m of maturing HRA loans planned inside the discount window that closed at March 2026 — the denominator will have lifted around the same long-dated stock, and the 52% is likely to have moved back inside range without the exposure in pounds needing to change.

The H1 2025/26 investment position looks strong. £257,497 received to 30 September 2025 against a £186,800 full-year budget is already 138% of plan in six months. The MMF balance had grown from £6.24m at 01 April to £10.23m at Q2 end, and MMF rates over the same period slid from 4.53% to 4.06%, so it was the volume effect carrying the position rather than the rate. Related, the interest-rate exposure indicator at page 6 has a 1% rise scoring an £84k revenue benefit rather than a cost — consistent with fixed-rate PWLB on the debt side and variable-rate MMF on the cash side, and it shows in what the H1 income has done for you.

We price every published PWLB book daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis, and the same page tracks the HRA rate against certainty and against gilts daily — indicative only, and only the DMO can quote. One standing point because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151: the liability benchmark pathway becomes central, and an interactive version is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. In your case, where 90% of the PWLB stock and 76% of the CFR sits on the HRA, the LB pathway is largely an HRA question, and the tool splits GF and HRA views.

One thing on our own side worth flagging: our loan file for Gosport currently doesn't line up with your 31 March table cleanly enough for us to quote a reconciliation back to you. We're working on it; disclosing it because we'd rather flag it than gloss it, not asking you to act on it.

On training, three fit the paper. Maturity structure and refinancing risk in practice picks up the page-6 indicator directly. HRA borrowing and the discounted PWLB rate covers the window that closed in March. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice sits behind the CFR-to-benchmark shape. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if any of it is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management Update, Policy and Organisation Board, 26 November 2025, at https://Gosport.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s6323/13-treasury-management-update.pdf.
